question: How do I hire a fractional CRO in Savannah?
body:
## Direct Answer
To hire a fractional CRO in Savannah, define the specific revenue problem you need solved, decide between a local Savannah-based operator and a remote fractional executive, then source candidates through executive fractional networks, RevOps communities, and warm referrals before running a scorecard-based interview. Expect a part-time engagement priced by day rate or monthly retainer, structured around a 90-day plan with clear revenue outcomes rather than a vague advisory relationship.

A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives a Savannah company senior go-to-market leadership without the cost or commitment of a full-time executive. For a growing manufacturer on the ports corridor, a logistics firm, a regional SaaS company, or a professional-services practice, the right fractional CRO can install pipeline discipline, fix a broken sales-to-marketing handoff, and build a forecast leadership can trust — usually in one or two days a week. The trick is hiring for a defined mandate, not a title, and structuring the engagement so you can measure whether it worked. The sections below walk the full path in order: what the role actually delivers, whether to weight local or remote candidates, where the qualified operators actually surface, how the money and contract should be structured, and how to interview so you can tell an operator from a talker before you sign anything.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a Savannah business?
A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue engine on a part-time basis: sales, marketing alignment, revenue operations, pricing, and often customer success. Unlike a consultant who diagnoses and hands you a slide deck, a fractional CRO is an operator who sits inside your leadership team, carries a number, and is accountable for moving it. In a Savannah context that might mean helping a port-adjacent logistics company move from relationship-based selling to a repeatable pipeline, or helping a Pooler-based B2B software startup build its first real sales motion so the founder can step out of every deal.

The scope varies with company stage. An early-stage firm usually needs the fractional CRO to build foundational systems — a CRM that people actually use, a defined sales stage model, a lead-to-close process, and a weekly cadence. A more established Savannah company that already has reps but flat growth typically needs diagnosis and repair: why win rates are slipping, why the forecast is always wrong, why marketing leads never convert. Because the engagement is part-time, the strongest fractional CROs resist doing the work themselves and instead build the muscle inside your existing team so the results survive after they leave. If you are still deciding whether the role you need is strategic leadership or hands-on execution, the distinction between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant is worth mapping before you write a single job description — see [pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vs-consultant](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vs-consultant).

It helps to be concrete about what the first ninety days usually produce, because "owns the revenue engine" is abstract until you see the deliverables. In practice a strong fractional CRO leaves behind a written revenue diagnosis (where deals actually leak, and why), a cleaned-up sales stage model with exit criteria for each stage, a forecast method leadership can defend to a bank or a board, a weekly pipeline-review cadence that the sales team runs without being babysat, and a compensation or territory adjustment where the numbers demand it. For a Savannah manufacturer or distributor that has grown on the strength of a few long-tenured relationship sellers, the highest-value early work is often simply making the revenue legible — turning tribal knowledge locked in one veteran rep's head into a documented process the next three hires can follow. That legibility is what lets an owner eventually sell the business, raise capital, or take a vacation without the pipeline going dark.

Just as important is what a fractional CRO should *not* do, because scope creep is the fastest way to waste the engagement. A fractional CRO is not a full-time sales rep who carries their own bag of accounts, is not a marketing agency, and is not a permanent crutch the team leans on forever. If you find the operator personally closing your deals month after month instead of teaching your reps to close, the engagement has quietly failed at its real job — building durable capability. The right operator is deliberately working to make themselves less necessary over time, and a good one will say so out loud in the first meeting.

## Should I hire a local Savannah fractional CRO or go remote?
The honest answer for most Savannah companies is that the talent pool for genuine fractional CROs is national, and constraining your search to the Savannah metro will shrink your candidate list far more than it helps. Fractional executive work went fully remote-friendly during the last several years, and the best operators run engagements across time zones without issue. That said, there are real reasons to weight local candidates: if your revenue motion is field-heavy — outside sales calling on regional accounts, trade-show-driven demand, or relationship selling into the Southeast — someone who can be in the room for quarterly business reviews and ride along on key accounts brings value a Zoom-only operator cannot.

The practical middle path most Savannah businesses land on is a "remote-first, on-site when it matters" arrangement: a fractional CRO who works primarily remotely but commits to being physically present for the kickoff, quarterly planning, and any high-stakes customer or board meetings. Savannah's proximity to Atlanta, Charleston, and Jacksonville also widens the pool of operators who can drive or take a short flight for periodic on-site work without charging full relocation-level travel. The diagram below shows how to reason through the local-versus-remote decision based on your revenue motion.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start hiring decision] --> B{Is your sales motion field heavy}
    B -->|Yes outside sales and events| C{Do you need in person QBRs}
    B -->|No inside sales and digital| D[Remote fractional CRO is fine]
    C -->|Yes| E[Prefer local or regional operator]
    C -->|No| F[Remote first with occasional on site]
    D --> G[Widen search nationally]
    F --> G
    E --> H[Search Savannah plus Atlanta and Charleston]
    G --> I[Score candidates on outcomes]
    H --> I
```

Do not let geography become the primary filter. A fractional CRO who has fixed the exact revenue problem you have — in your industry, at your stage — is worth far more than a nearby generalist. Rank fit and track record first, then treat location as a tie-breaker. For a deeper look at structuring the engagement once you have candidates, the guide on [pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-exec-engagement-models](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-exec-engagement-models) walks through retainer versus day-rate tradeoffs.

There is also an industry-knowledge dimension to the local question that owners often miss. A fractional CRO who has never touched logistics may take a month just to learn how freight brokerage margins work, how port seasonality moves demand, or why a manufacturing sales cycle stretches across procurement committees — and you are paying senior rates for that ramp. In that scenario, a remote operator who has run revenue for three logistics companies will out-produce a local generalist from day one, even though they are eight hundred miles away. The reverse is also true: for a Savannah professional-services firm whose growth depends on being visibly plugged into the coastal Georgia business community — chamber events, local referral networks, face-to-face trust — a well-connected regional operator's rolodex can be worth more than deep vertical expertise. Weigh which of those two levers, vertical experience or local presence, actually drives your revenue, and let that decide where on the local-to-remote spectrum you land. Most companies discover the vertical lever matters more than they assumed.

## Where do I actually find qualified fractional CRO candidates?
Sourcing is where most Savannah owners stall, because fractional CROs rarely apply to job postings — they get referred. Start with your warm network: other founders and CEOs in the Savannah and coastal Georgia business community, your board or advisors, your investors if you have them, and your accountant or fractional CFO, who often knows the fractional executive circle. A single strong referral from someone who watched a fractional CRO deliver is worth more than fifty cold profiles. The Savannah Economic Development Authority, the local chamber, and regional CEO peer groups are all reasonable places to ask for names.

Beyond referrals, there are structured channels. Fractional executive marketplaces and staffing networks specifically place part-time CROs and VPs of Sales. RevOps and go-to-market communities — Pavilion, RevGenius, and similar operator networks — are full of people who do fractional work or can point you to someone who does. LinkedIn search for "Fractional CRO" or "Fractional VP Sales" with a Southeast filter will surface operators, and their content usually reveals how they think. Recruiters who specialize in revenue leadership can run a fractional search, though they add cost. The workflow below shows a sourcing funnel that consistently produces qualified candidates.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Define the revenue problem] --> B[Ask warm network for referrals]
    A --> C[Post in RevOps communities]
    A --> D[Search fractional marketplaces]
    B --> E[Build candidate shortlist]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Screen for stage and industry fit]
    F --> G[Run scorecard interviews]
    G --> H[Reference check on outcomes]
    H --> I[Structured paid trial or pilot]
```

Whatever channel you use, insist on evidence. Ask every candidate for two or three specific engagements where they owned a number, what the starting state was, and what changed measurably. Fractional work attracts both elite operators and people between full-time jobs who are waiting out the market — the difference shows up fast when you ask for concrete before-and-after outcomes and then call the references to confirm them.

A useful discipline is to build a shortlist of five to seven candidates from at least two different channels rather than falling for the first warm referral who sounds impressive. Sourcing from a single channel tends to produce a monoculture — five operators who all learned the same playbook at the same kind of company — and you want enough variety to see genuinely different approaches to your problem. As you build the list, watch for a few reliable red flags: an operator who pitches you a solution before they understand your business, one who wants to run everything themselves rather than build your team, one whose "case studies" are all vague ("drove significant growth") with no numbers you can verify, and one who is clearly juggling so many concurrent clients that your two days a week would realistically get one. A serious fractional CRO limits how many engagements they take precisely because the work requires real embedded attention, so ask directly how many clients they currently serve and how they protect each one's time. The answer tells you a lot about whether you will actually get a leader or just a name on a retainer.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost, and how should I structure the deal?
Fractional CRO pricing generally follows one of three models: a monthly retainer for a set number of days, a day rate billed against actual work, or an outcome-linked structure that blends a base retainer with a bonus tied to revenue milestones. Retainers are the most common because they give both sides predictability — you know your monthly cost, and the operator knows the commitment. Day rates suit shorter or more variable engagements. Rather than fixating on a single number, benchmark several candidates against each other and against the fully loaded cost of a full-time CRO hire, which includes base, bonus, equity, benefits, and recruiting fees. The whole point of "fractional" is that you pay for a slice of senior capacity instead of the entire package.

Structure the deal around outcomes and time, not vibes. A strong engagement letter names the specific mandate — for example, "build a repeatable outbound motion and a forecast leadership trusts within two quarters" — the number of days per week or month, the reporting cadence, the systems and team the CRO will touch, and a clear exit or renewal checkpoint. Many Savannah companies start with a paid diagnostic sprint of two to four weeks before committing to a longer retainer; this de-risks the relationship for both sides and gives you a real working sample rather than an interview impression. Always define what success looks like in measurable terms up front, and build in a 90-day review so you can course-correct or walk away cleanly. For how to write revenue outcomes into the agreement itself, see [pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-leader-scorecard](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-leader-scorecard).

Be deliberate about the outcome-linked portion if you use one, because badly designed incentives can quietly warp behavior. Tying a bonus purely to booked revenue in the same quarter can push an operator toward discounting deals or pulling forward pipeline that would have closed anyway, neither of which builds durable value. Smarter outcome triggers reward the things a fractional CRO can actually control and that compound over time: forecast accuracy within a tolerance band, an improvement in win rate on a defined segment, pipeline coverage reaching a healthy multiple of quota, or the successful hire and ramp of the first two salespeople. Cash-flow reality also matters for a smaller Savannah business — a retainer is a fixed monthly line item you must fund regardless of a slow month, so make sure the engagement is scoped to a level of days you can sustain for the full expected duration rather than a heavy start you cannot afford to continue. And put the unglamorous terms in writing too: confidentiality, ownership of any playbooks or CRM configurations the CRO builds (they should belong to your company, not walk out the door), a notice period, and what happens to in-flight work if either side exits early. Those clauses feel like lawyer-tax when the relationship is warm, and they are exactly what protect you when it cools.

## How do I evaluate and interview a fractional CRO?
Interview a fractional CRO the way you would evaluate an operator, not an advisor — with a scorecard tied to the outcomes you need. Before the first conversation, write down the two or three revenue problems that would justify the entire engagement, then design your questions to test whether this person has actually solved them. Instead of asking "what's your philosophy on sales," ask "walk me through the last time you inherited a broken forecast — what did you find, what did you change, and what was the number ninety days later." Operators who have done the work answer in specifics: stages, conversion rates, cadences, named systems. People who have only theorized answer in frameworks and adjectives.

Run at least one working session, not just interviews. Give a shortlisted candidate a redacted look at your pipeline or a real problem and ask them to talk through how they would diagnose and attack it. You are testing three things: whether they can quickly find the real constraint, whether they can teach and lead your existing team rather than sideline it, and whether they will be honest with you when the news is bad. Then check references hard — call people who managed them and people they managed, and ask specifically about outcomes and accountability, not just whether they were pleasant to work with. A fractional CRO who is genuinely good will welcome a paid pilot and a reference-heavy process, because it is exactly how they win the engagements worth having.

Pay close attention to the cultural fit alongside the competence, because a fractional CRO succeeds only if your existing team lets them lead. The best operator in the world will stall if your veteran sales manager treats them as an outside threat, so watch in the working session for how the candidate handles disagreement, whether they build rapport with the people who would actually execute their plan, and whether they show respect for what your team already does well rather than sweeping in to declare everything broken. Ask your own key people to sit in on part of the process and tell you honestly whether they would follow this person. It is also worth being explicit in the interview about the exit — a strong fractional CRO has a clear point of view on how the engagement should end, whether that is transitioning to a full-time hire they help you recruit, tapering to a lighter advisory cadence, or handing a self-sustaining system to your internal team. An operator who cannot describe how they make themselves unnecessary is one who may quietly design the engagement to run forever, and that is the opposite of what fractional leadership is supposed to buy you.

## Related questions
### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a VP of Sales?
A fractional CRO owns the full revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and often customer success — and works part-time across strategy and systems. A VP of Sales typically owns the sales team and quota execution, usually full-time and narrower in scope.

### How long does a fractional CRO engagement usually last?
Most run six to eighteen months. The common arc is a short diagnostic sprint, a build-and-fix phase across two to four quarters, then a transition to either a full-time hire or a lighter advisory cadence once the systems and team are self-sustaining.

### Can a small Savannah business afford a fractional CRO?
Often yes — that is the model's purpose. You pay for a fraction of senior capacity, typically one to two days a week, instead of a full executive package, which makes seasoned revenue leadership accessible to companies that could never fund a full-time CRO.

### Should I hire a fractional CRO or a sales consultant first?
Hire a fractional CRO when you need someone accountable for a number and embedded in your leadership team. Hire a consultant when you need a one-time diagnosis or a specific project. The CRO owns outcomes; the consultant delivers recommendations.

### When should I convert a fractional CRO to full-time?
Convert when revenue is predictable enough to justify a full-time salary and the role now requires daily presence — hiring, managing a growing team, and day-to-day operations. Many fractional CROs will help recruit their own full-time successor as part of the exit.

## FAQ
**Do I need a fractional CRO based in Savannah specifically?**
No. The talent pool is national and most engagements run remote-first. Prefer local or regional candidates only if your motion is field-heavy and needs frequent in-person presence; otherwise rank track record and industry fit above location.

**What industries in Savannah benefit most from a fractional CRO?**
Logistics and port-adjacent services, regional manufacturing, B2B SaaS, healthcare services, and professional-services firms all benefit — essentially any company with a repeatable sales motion, a real revenue target, and a gap in senior go-to-market leadership.

**How many hours per week does a fractional CRO work?**
Typically one to two days a week, though it flexes with the phase of the engagement. Kickoff and diagnostic periods are more intensive; steady-state coaching and cadence management require less. Define the day commitment in the engagement letter.

**How do I measure whether the fractional CRO is working?**
Tie success to leading and lagging indicators agreed up front: pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, win rate, sales-cycle length, and net new revenue. Review at 30, 60, and 90 days against those specific numbers rather than general impressions.

**What should be in a fractional CRO engagement contract?**
The specific mandate and success metrics, days per week or month, reporting cadence, systems and team in scope, pricing model, confidentiality and IP terms, and a defined review-and-exit checkpoint. Keep it outcome-oriented, not open-ended.

**Can a fractional CRO help hire my sales team?**
Yes. Building the team is often core to the mandate — defining roles, writing scorecards, interviewing, onboarding, and setting comp plans. A good fractional CRO builds a team that outlasts the engagement rather than one dependent on them.

**How is a fractional CRO different from an interim CRO?**
An interim CRO is a full-time placeholder filling a temporary vacancy until a permanent hire lands. A fractional CRO is a permanent part-time arrangement by design — ongoing senior leadership at a fraction of the time and cost.

**What is the biggest mistake when hiring a fractional CRO?**
Hiring for the title instead of a defined problem. Without a specific mandate and measurable outcomes, the engagement drifts into vague advising, and you cannot tell whether it worked. Define the revenue problem first, then hire against it.

**How soon should I expect results from a fractional CRO?**
Expect diagnosis and quick structural fixes within the first 30 to 60 days, and measurable movement in leading indicators like pipeline coverage and forecast accuracy by 90 days. Durable revenue lift usually shows across two to four quarters as the new systems and cadence compound.
